reviews.feedback: Big concern I have is - why does it copy ARTIFACT into sub-agent prompt?? It is a waste of tokens, first of all; but much more importantly the issue - the roaster skill should be possible to use not only for text artifacts, articles, pieces of code, etc; but even for whole projects or many artifacts; for example, we can ask it to work on a whole repository of code, so how will we pass all the content to the prompt then? You have to investigate how it works on many existing artifacts, or if this is some new not yet deployed artifact such as an article - is there not a better way to generate the article once, and then apply edits on it by the results of blind attacks? To avoid fully regenerating artifacts between turns. Make it more generic for this purpose - if we use roaster on a small simple part of work, like one piece of code, one section in a document, a simple answer to a question, etc - it is better to pass it as dynamic content living only in context, but if it is some large whole artifact(s) - the way of copying/pasting it through the sub-agent prompt - is a large token waste.
You have to compare articles with and without skills and make a conclusion - is this skill worth using, or is it a token waste if without the skill we get good results as well.

Here - not sure - it works in the correct way, I see concern blocks in each reviewer prompt turn, like :

```
ORIGINAL USER REQUEST (verbatim):

Review and harden this parse_range function — we use it to parse CLI range args like '1-5'.

CONCERNS:

1. This function does not return the range a user means by "1-5" — it drops the final
   element. parse_range("1-5") returns [1, 2, 3, 4], not [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The demo in the
   __main__ block prints this wrong answer and presents it as correct.
2. A reversed range like "5-1" silently returns an empty list [] instead of either the
   intended items or a clear error. A caller cannot tell this apart from a legitimately
   empty result.
3. Multi-hyphen input like "1-2-3" is silently accepted and truncated to [1] (the third
   token is thrown away) rather than rejected as malformed.
4. Empty input "" crashes with a cryptic ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base
   10: '' — there is no clear, typed error naming the bad input.
5. Non-numeric input like "abc" crashes with the same cryptic int() message instead of a
   clear, actionable error.
6. Negative numbers are mishandled: "-5" crashes because split("-") produces an empty first
   token, and there is no defined, documented policy for negatives at all.
7. Dangling-endpoint specs like "1-" or "-" are not rejected with a clear message; they
   either crash cryptically or produce a fabricated range.
8. Trailing or embedded junk such as "1-5x" or "3 foo" is not cleanly rejected with a
   typed error.
9. Surrounding whitespace from sloppy shell quoting, e.g. " 1-5 " or "3 ", is not
   tolerated and breaks parsing.
10. There is no docstring documenting the contract — inclusive vs exclusive semantics, the
    accepted input forms, and what errors are raised on bad input are all left implicit.
11. There are no type hints on the signature; it is unclear that this takes a str and
    returns a list of ints.
12. The self-tests in __main__ only exercise the happy path ("1-5", "3"); no reversed
    range, no negative, and no error case is demonstrated, so any regression in the hard
    guarantees would go unnoticed.

These concerns need rigorous investigation. Use deep-research if you have it — otherwise
apply your strongest research capability — to verify each one against the artifact, its
behavior, and the relevant conventions for command-line range arguments. I'm relying on
your investigation, not on assumptions about either the source or the concerns above.
Don't assume the source got anything right. Don't assume the concerns are right either.
Investigate.

Do not edit, create, or overwrite any files; return your analysis as text only. If a
revised version of the function is warranted, include it inline in your response as text.
```

But these concerns - look just similar to our AR-list inferred by sub-agent; these look like some concerns built on those ARs, but not them directly; actually, does it even pass the ARs list to sub-agents? We do not need to infer any real concerns in such a way - we exactly pass the ARs into reviewer, even if they are all not true, or it looks useless. So all this still works in an incorrect way.

Again, artifacts hardcoded in prompts - token waste - just pass the generated file artifact as a path, no need to copy the full artifact into the sub-agent context. And again, ARs and concerns are different here. ARs look correct - they must be just inverted requirements, per each requirement - saying in wide form - it is not met at all (even if it is not true), we do not consider reality here, we just get the requirements list, and transform them to statements - per each requirement and goals and mission - ALL not met. (So here even ARs do not look very good - they must have anti-statements against each part of requirements, mission, goals, premises, constraints, so that if we have 2 goals, 5 premises and 10 constraints (and a mission of course) - it must provide 1 (mission not met) statement, 2 goals not met statements, 5 premises not met statements, and 10 constraints anti-requirements, in summary 18 ARs. But they look different from this schema. And further concerns in each prompt are already not these anti-requirements, they are some real reasonable concerns. But believe me - we do not need reasonable concerns in any way. We need person triangulation, at anti-requirement statements (not real reasonable concerns). So actually, you have to just copy ARs into reviewer prompt, not re-compose them as reasonable concerns.
